1387.title: Maharashtra's Varkari
1387.hook: the walk is over, the line to the god stretches out of sight, and some pilgrims bow to the temple's spire and turn for home
1387.howItsDone: At Pandharpur, Varkaris bathe in the Chandrabhaga, wait for darshan of Vitthal, where pilgrims may touch his feet, or bow to the temple's pinnacle from outside, then return home.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Maharashtra's Varkari and the road's singers: Janabai at the grindstone, Chokhamela outside the walls.

After all those days of walking, the town comes into view: Pandharpur, on the bank of the river. The dindis pour in, the palkhis arrive, and the singing gets louder, not softer. Then the walkers see the line to stand before Vitthal. It winds through the streets and out of sight. Some will wait in it for many hours. And some, the story of the road says, walk down to the river, bathe, look up at the temple's spire, bow, and turn for home, content. Today, the end of the road, and what counts as arriving.
screen: `PANDHARPUR COMES INTO VIEW.` → `A LINE OUT OF SIGHT.` → `A BOW TO THE SPIRE.`

segments.voice: The river at Pandharpur is the Bhima, and here Varkaris call it the Chandrabhaga, because, tradition says, it bends like a crescent moon. Pilgrims bathe in it first. Then the town fills with singing all through the night, and on the holy day itself, the Ekadashi, the crowd reaches its peak. Inside the temple, Vitthal stands on his brick, hands on hips, the way Pundalik left him. And pilgrims are allowed close enough to lay their heads on his feet. Not only to see him. To touch. A child running to a mother doesn't stop at arm's length. But the line is long, and not everyone reaches the feet. So Varkari tradition holds that seeing the kalas, the temple's pinnacle, from outside is darshan too, a true seeing of the god. The tradition makes room for both. At the temple's entrance is a step called Namdev's step. Tradition says Namdev asked to be laid there, so that every pilgrim's feet would touch him on the way to Vitthal. Nearby, tradition places Chokhamela's samadhi: the singer who stood outside the walls now rests at the door. So the saints are already there, under the feet of the crowd, still pointing in. Then the walkers go home, back to fields and shops and kitchens, until the next wari. The arriving was never meant to be the whole of it. Tomorrow, far north, to Kashmir.
screen: `A BATH IN THE CHANDRABHAGA` · `A HEAD ON VITTHAL'S FEET` · `THE SPIRE IS DARSHAN TOO` · `NAMDEV'S STEP, THEN HOME`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been working toward for a long time, a road you're still on, and stop for a moment, as if you'd just seen the spire from the riverbank. Notice where you are, right now, without needing to be any closer. If you pray, you can bow inwardly, from wherever you're standing.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The walkers who reach Pandharpur, bow at Vitthal's feet or to his spire, step over Namdev's step, and go home until the next wari. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. A bow to the spire counts as arriving too. Until tomorrow, in Kashmir.

1388.title: Kashmir
1388.hook: before the valley there was a lake, and in the lake a demon who could not be caught while he stayed in the water
1388.howItsDone: Kashmiri Hindus tell the story of Satisar, the lake drained so the demon Jalodbhava could be defeated, as the beginning of the valley, and honor its springs and rivers as sacred.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharashtra's Varkari road ended at Pandharpur: a bow at Vitthal's feet, or to his spire, and then home.

Before there was a valley, the old book says, there was a lake. Mountains all around, and water filling the space between them, still and deep. And in that water lived a demon. As long as he stayed in the lake, nobody could touch him; he came out to raid the lands nearby and slipped back under the surface. The gods couldn't reach him. So how do you defeat someone who hides in the water? You take away the water. This week, Kashmir, and the story it tells about how it began.
screen: `A LAKE BETWEEN MOUNTAINS.` → `A DEMON HIDING IN THE WATER.` → `TAKE AWAY THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The book is the Nilamata Purana, a Sanskrit text of Kashmir, and here it is in paraphrase. The lake was called Satisar, the lake of Sati, the goddess. The demon in it was Jalodbhava. He couldn't be killed in his element, so the sage Kashyapa went to the gods and asked for help. Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma came. The mountain wall was opened, the water drained away, and the demon, left on dry ground, was struck down. What was left behind was a green valley, and people came to live in it. Tradition links Kashmir's name with Kashyapa, the sage who asked. It's a story about a place, and it treats the land itself as sacred. The valley's floor was once the goddess's lake. Its rivers and springs that remained are holy, and this week keeps meeting holy water in Kashmir. Look at the shape of the victory, too. The gods don't fight the demon in the water. They change the ground under him. Some readers hear an inner meaning: what lurks under the surface of a mind loses its power once it's brought into the open. In time Kashmir became known as a home of poets and thinkers, some of whom you've met already this year in the Shiva Sutras and in Lal Ded. This week, more of them, starting from the lake.
screen: `THE LAKE OF SATI` · `JALODBHAVA IN THE WATER` · `KASHYAPA ASKS, THE LAKE DRAINS` · `A HOLY VALLEY`

segments.voice: Picture a lake between mountains, its surface flat and calm, and with each out-breath let the water level drop a little. Whatever has been sitting under the surface of your mind today, a worry, a grudge, a plan, just see it in the open, without fighting it. If you pray, you can offer it up in your own way.
Kashmir. The valley that, the Nilamata Purana says, was once the lake of Sati, drained when the sage Kashyapa asked the gods for help. Today's word.
Your line: Kashmir. A valley that began, the story says, as a holy lake. Until tomorrow.

1389.title: Kashmir
1389.hook: a poet sits down to write the story of his valley's kings, and the first rule he sets himself is to be like a judge
1389.howItsDone: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is read in Sanskrit and in translation as the chronicle of Kashmir's kings; Kashmiri Hindus treasure it as the valley's own story, beginning from the lake of Satisar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir began as a lake: Satisar, drained at the sage Kashyapa's asking, with the demon left on dry ground.

A poet in Kashmir has a big job ahead of him. He's going to tell the story of the valley's kings, the good and the cruel, the wise and the foolish, in Sanskrit verse. Before he starts, he sets himself a rule. A poet who tells the past, he says, deserves praise only if his words are like a judge's: free of love and free of hate. No flattery for a patron. No revenge on an enemy. The poet's name is Kalhana. His book is the Rajatarangini, the river of kings.
screen: `A POET AND A VALLEY OF KINGS.` → `LIKE A JUDGE.` → `THE RIVER OF KINGS.`

segments.voice: Kalhana's book opens with verses honoring Shiva, then turns to the valley and tells yesterday's lake again: the water of Satisar drained and the land made ready for people. From there it runs on, king after king, like a river. That's the picture in the title: kings rising and passing like waves on moving water. Kalhana doesn't pretend the kings were all heroes. He tells of greed and plots and wasted lives alongside generosity and good rule. That's what his rule about the judge is for. If you love one side or hate another, you bend the story. He wants it straight. He also says he didn't make it up from nothing: he read older chronicles and records before him, and pieced them together. Then comes something a reader might not look for in a history. Kalhana says the mood he wants the whole work to leave behind is calm: in the language of Indian poetics, the rasa of shanta, peace. Why calm, for a story full of kings? Because if you watch power rise and fall long enough, you stop gripping it. The waves come and go. The river keeps moving. So it's a history, yes, but read as a long lesson in letting go. Fitting, in a valley that tells its beginning as a lake. Even the kings are water here. They rise, and they pass.
screen: `A HISTORY THAT OPENS WITH SHIVA` · `TOLD LIKE A JUDGE` · `PIECED FROM OLDER RECORDS` · `ITS MOOD IS CALM`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one recent disagreement and tell yourself its story as Kalhana would, without love and without hate: what happened, plainly, and what each person did. Notice where you want to bend it, straighten it a little without scolding yourself, and then let the whole thing pass like a wave on moving water.
Kashmir. The valley whose kings Kalhana set down in the Rajatarangini, the river of kings, told like a judge and meant to leave the reader calm. Today's word.

1390.title: Kashmir
1390.hook: a theater audience weeps at a tragedy and walks out into the night strangely at peace, and a Kashmiri teacher asks why
1390.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism and of Indian poetics read Abhinavagupta's writings with teachers, and his account of rasa is still taught to students of classical dance, music and theater.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir, Kalhana's river of kings, told like a judge and meant to leave the reader calm.

On stage, a grieving lover cries out, and down in the seats people are wiping their eyes. Then the play ends, the lamps go out, and they walk home under the stars, talking quietly, somehow lighter than when they came. Nobody died in their house tonight. They wept anyway, and it did them good. Why does a sad story feel like a gift? A teacher in Kashmir thought hard about that question, and his answer reached all the way to Shiva. His name is Abhinavagupta.
screen: `TEARS IN THE THEATER.` → `LIGHTER ON THE WAY HOME.` → `ABHINAVAGUPTA ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Abhinavagupta is remembered as a teacher who wrote about two things that might seem far apart: the art of theater and poetry, and the way to Shiva. In his tradition they turn out to be close. Start with the theater. Indian poetics speaks of rasa, the taste of a work of art. In a tragedy there's real sorrow in the story, but it isn't your private sorrow. You don't have to fix anything or protect anyone. So the feeling comes to you loosened from your own small worries, and you can savor it, the way you savor a flavor. That's rasa. In that moment, Abhinavagupta explained, the viewer's little self, my problems, my plans, steps aside, and what's left is a kind of open, tasting awareness, with a quality of rest and wonder. Then he made the bold link. If a play can briefly lift us into wide, delighted awareness, that awareness isn't something the play adds. It was there all along. And in his Shaiva teaching, that wide awareness is what Shiva is. The theater gives a glimpse, borrowed, for an evening. The path is about seeing it without the borrowing. Tradition adds an ending to his own story: one day he walked into a cave with his disciples, chanting, and was not seen again. Kalhana's river flowed toward calm. Abhinavagupta's road runs through a theater, to the same quiet.
screen: `THEATER AND SHIVA, TOGETHER` · `RASA: THE TASTE OF ART` · `THE SMALL SELF STEPS ASIDE` · `THE AWARENESS WAS ALWAYS THERE`

segments.voice: Let a little of the feeling from a song, a film or a story that once moved you return. Then gently notice what's noticing it: the feeling comes and goes, but something is aware of it the whole time, wide and quiet. Rest there, in the tasting, without needing the feeling to stay.
Kashmir. The valley where Abhinavagupta taught that the taste of a play, the rasa, is a glimpse of the wide awareness his tradition calls Shiva. Today's word.
Your line: Kashmir. On this view, the quiet behind every play was there all along. Same time tomorrow.

1391.title: Kashmir
1391.hook: a woman has longed for a man she's only heard described; he stands in front of her, and nothing happens, until someone says, that's him
1391.howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism study Utpaladeva's teaching on recognition with a teacher, and his hymns to Shiva are read and recited as devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir, Abhinavagupta and rasa: the taste of a play, and the wide awareness doing the tasting.

A young woman has fallen in love with a man she's never met. She's only heard about him: how kind he is, how he speaks, what he's done. She thinks about him all the time. Then one day he comes to her house and stands right in front of her. And she feels nothing much; he's just a visitor. Until someone at her side leans over and says: that's him. Everything changes, though not one thing in the room has moved. A teacher in Kashmir used that story to explain what he meant by recognition.
screen: `IN LOVE WITH SOMEONE UNMET.` → `HE STANDS IN FRONT OF HER.` → `THAT'S HIM.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Utpaladeva, a Shaiva thinker of Kashmir, and the story comes, in paraphrase, from his work on recognition. That word is the key: pratyabhijna. Not finding something new. Recognizing what's already in front of you. In his teaching, Shiva isn't far off. Shiva is the very awareness you're living in, the one who sees and knows, right now. So the problem was never that God is missing. It's like the woman in the story: her beloved is standing in the room, and she's still longing, because she hasn't recognized him. Nothing needs to be brought in. Something needs to be seen. Look at what makes the difference: someone at her side who says, that's him. In Utpaladeva's tradition, that's the role of a teacher and of teaching. The teacher doesn't hand you a new self. The teacher points. Notice the joy, too. She doesn't get a lecture on who he is. The recognition itself is the delight. And Utpaladeva also wrote hymns to Shiva, full of longing and tenderness, and the two belong together: the more you see that he's here, the more there is to sing about. The week's Kashmir has been building this way: a valley drained so a hidden thing could be seen, a history told without bending, a theater where the small self steps aside, and now a woman who simply recognizes who's in the room.
screen: `PRATYABHIJNA: RECOGNITION` · `THE BELOVED ALREADY IN THE ROOM` · `THE TEACHER POINTS: THAT'S HIM` · `RECOGNITION IS THE DELIGHT`

segments.voice: Notice that you're aware: of sounds, of the breath, of the body sitting, without hunting for anything new. Whenever the mind goes looking somewhere else, come back and say quietly inside: already here. If you pray, you can turn to God as already present, in your own way.
Kashmir. The valley where Utpaladeva taught recognition: the beloved is already in the room, and the teacher simply points. Today's word.

1392.title: Kashmir
1392.hook: a bowl of rice pudding set down beside a spring, for a goddess who lives in the water
1392.howItsDone: At the Kheer Bhawani shrine at Tulmul, near Srinagar, devotees offer kheer, milk and flowers at the spring around the shrine, and Kashmiri Pandit families gather there on the goddess's festival day.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir, Utpaladeva and recognition: the beloved already standing in the room. Today i leave the books for a while and go to the water.

A bowl of rice pudding, cooked slowly in milk, carried in two hands down a path under tall trees. At the end of the path there's a spring, and in the middle of the spring, a small shrine. People bend at the edge of the water and offer the pudding, kheer, and milk, and flowers. Then they do something you might not expect at a temple. They look down, carefully, at the color of the water. Today, the goddess of the spring at Tulmul, and why people read her water.
screen: `A BOWL OF KHEER` → `A SHRINE IN A SPRING` → `LOOKING AT THE WATER`

segments.voice: The shrine stands in a village called Tulmul, not far from Srinagar. The goddess there is called Ragnya, or Maharagnya, a form of the Mother. She also goes by a homelier name: Kheer Bhawani, Bhawani of the rice pudding, because of what her devotees bring her. Bhawani is a name of the Goddess, the wife of Shiva, so the name holds the kitchen and the heavens together. The shrine isn't on a hill or behind a gate. It sits in the water, and the water is the point. Tradition says the spring changes color. Pilgrims say that clear, light shades are a good sign, and that dark shades have been read as a warning of hard times for the valley. Some take that as a plain wonder. Others hear something quieter: a community that keeps watching the same water together, year after year, and talks about what it sees. The goddess of Tulmul is especially dear to Kashmiri Pandits, the Hindu community of the valley. Tradition holds her festival day as a homecoming, and families who now live far from Kashmir still try to come back to the spring for it, carrying milk and pudding the way their grandparents did. A temple can be a place you visit. This one is also a place you return to.

1393.title: Kashmir
1393.hook: walnuts soaking in pots of water through Shiva's great night, then handed out to the neighbors
1393.howItsDone: Kashmiri Pandit families keep Herath at home with an overnight worship of the vatuk, pots of water and walnuts honored as Shiva and his company, and afterward share the soaked walnuts with relatives and neighbors as prasad.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir, the spring at Tulmul, where pilgrims bring rice pudding and read the color of the water.

A kitchen in winter. On a clean cloth, a row of pots, filled to the brim with water, and in the water, walnuts, still in their shells. Someone has drawn on the pots and hung flowers around their necks. The family will sit up with them tonight, singing, worshiping, keeping the lamp going. In a day or two, those walnuts will be soft from the water and on their way to every relative and neighbor on the list. Today, the last of the Kashmir days: Herath, Shiva's great night, kept the Kashmiri way.
screen: `POTS OF WATER AND WALNUTS` → `A NIGHT KEPT AWAKE` → `HERATH`

segments.voice: You met Mahashivaratri in year one: the great night of Shiva, kept with fasting and worship and staying awake. Kashmiri Pandits keep it too, and they call it Herath. In their tradition it's a night kept at home, around the family, more than at a temple. The family sets out a pot and smaller vessels, filled with water and walnuts, and calls the arrangement the vatuk. It's worshiped as Shiva and the company around him. Families tell the meaning in different ways. Some speak of Shiva's wedding to Parvati, with the pots as the wedding guests. Others speak of Bhairava, a fierce form of Shiva, appearing as light. Nobody has to settle it tonight. The water, the flowers and the lamp do their work either way. When the worship is over, the soaked walnuts become prasad, a blessed gift, and they're shared out: to grandparents, to cousins, to the family next door. In the days after, people visit each other with greetings. So the night that begins alone with God ends at other people's doors. And that closes the week: the Varkaris reaching Pandharpur and turning for home, then Kashmir's drained lake, its river of kings, a theater, a recognition, a spring a community watches, and last, a holy night with a kitchen at its center.
